speechtext:

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext:
May I
direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Is it a fact that in a letter to the Minister of Finance on January 13, 1961, four days before the Columbia river treaty was signed in Washington on January 17, the premier of British Columbia warned the government that British Columbia could not agree to the financing aspects of the treaty and therefore would not be a party to the treaty?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minisler of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a letter was received from the premier of British Coumbia on the 17th, I think it was. I am speaking from recollection, having in mind the date of the treaty. If I recall correctly the treaty was signed in Washington on a Tuesday, and this letter arrived either that day or the day before. It could hardly be correctly construed, I think, in the manner in which the hon. member has construed it, in the light of the negotiations which had taken place up to that time between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: Would the minister table the letter from the premier, a part of which is quoted in the Vancouver Province of May 17, 1961?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: I will certainly be pleased to table the letter or any others for which there is consent of both governments.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: Would the minister inform the house if the receipt of this letter did not cause the government some concern at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext:
The letter arrived just at about the time of the signing of the treaty, and the signing of the treaty had been preceded by extended negotiations on a tripartite basis. British Columbia had been a party to the discussions which had proceeded between the governments of the United States and Canada. They were fully in accord with everything that was taking place in that regard. The letter which has been referred to was not interpreted as changing the situation in that respect, because the government of Canada was simply proceeding in the way that had been agreed upon by all three governments in the course of the discussions. There was no occasion at that time for any

disagreement or alteration of what had been accepted by all parties as a firm understanding among them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: Did the minister not state, as affirmed by the premier of British Columbia, that the letter was received before the treaty was signed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO LETTER FROM B.C. PREMIER
speechtext: The letter was received in Ottawa before the treaty was signed in Washington by, I think, a matter of a few hours.

Naturally I did not have the exact page in my memory, but my memory was accurate. I should like to quote these words, spoken by the secretary of state for external affairs of that day:
As far as trade with China is concerned, there is no argument on that score. speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister if he can say whether or not a cabinet committee has been established to deal with the threatened closure of three coal mines in Cape Breton, and whether the government has made an offer to Dosco to defray the cost of keeping the mines open?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ACTION BY CABINET RESPECTING MINE CLOSINGS
speechtext:
As to the first part of the question, may I say that the hon. gentleman, with his wide experience as clerk of the privy council and also as minister, must realize that the establishment of cabinet committees is not usually brought to the attention of the House of Commons.
As to the second question, the answer was given the other day by the Minister of Labour.

subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ACTION BY CABINET RESPECTING MINE CLOSINGS
speechtext: I wonder if I could put a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Is the Prime Minister aware that in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of Saturday a statement appears under the heading "Coal; Cabinet Committee of Five Set Up"? speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ACTION BY CABINET RESPECTING MINE CLOSINGS
speechtext: Order. The hon. member's question was, is the Prime Minister aware of a report in the newspaper, and then he proceeds to read the report. This is not in accordance with our practice, to read from a press report and ask whether or not the statement is correct. This is a practice that has not been accepted in the house. If there is a supplementary question arising out of the report, other than whether it is correct, perhaps the hon. member would put it.

subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ACTION BY CABINET RESPECTING MINE CLOSINGS

I am drawing Your
Honour's attention to the fact that I did not ask whether the report was correct. I am asking the Prime Minister whether he is aware of the fact that there is a report. speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: CAPE BRETON-ACTION BY CABINET RESPECTING MINE CLOSINGS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the
[Mr. Pickersgill.)

Minister of Agriculture. My question is prompted and spurred by the interest of numerous people in the maintenance and development of the economic family farm. In view of the decision at a meeting held in Winnipeg on April 24 and 25 of leaders from all branches of agricultural production and marketing to proceed to establish a national farm policy research council, will the minister inform the house whether his department was represented at this meeting and what assistance, advice or guidance his department intends to offer in the establishment of this urgently required research council?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO NATIONAL FARM POLICY RESEARCH COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time the government of Canada was examining into the question of a national agricultural program which was eventually announced in the house on August 30, 1958, by the Prime Minister, one of the gaps we discovered was some form of objective research into marketing and sociology. We set up an interdepartmental committee which recommended that some form of objective research group should be set up outside of the government and outside of the farm organizations.
At that time I approached several of the farm organizations in the west pointing out the need for this research group, and a group was set up among the farm organizations in the west which recommended that there should be a prairie agricultural economics research group. In the meantime the government of Manitoba, through its minister recommended, at the agriculture ministers' conference last October that there should be a research institute for all of Canada, and his government took the lead in calling a meeting of all governments and farm organizations for some time early this spring, which resulted in the meeting at the end of April that was mentioned by the hon. member.
At that meeting the government of Canada was represented by myself, with 11 officials from various departments, and a two day discussion took place. All the governments of Canada were represented, and all the farm organizations. A committee was instructed to prepare a plan by July 15 of this year which would be presented to the 11 governments and various farm organizations, and also to Agri-business. This report is due by July 15 of this year, at which time I would imagine the farm organizations will consult their organizations in full meeting and the agriculture ministers will deal with it either at the July meeting in Prince Edward Island or the November meeting here in Ottawa.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of the construction of the distant early warning line there was a rule against unnecessary contact with Eskimos. Many thousands of construction workers were rushed into the Arctic to complete the line in two years. In many areas of the north this was the first contact by the Eskimos with large numbers of people from south of the 60th parallel. Eskimos have low immunity to disease, and there was concern over the possibility of epidemics being brought in by construction workers from the outside, and also over the possibility of improper relations-I stress that word "improper"-that would have an adverse effect on the Eskimo people.
In March, 1955 the deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources wrote to the Western Electric Company, which was responsible for the construction of the D.E.W. line, regarding measures to protect the health and welfare of the Eskimos, and particularly with reference to reduction in the possibility of the spread of disease. When the agreement with the United States in respect of the
D.E.W. line was concluded in May, 1955, a clause was inserted designed to provide similar protection.
Conditions in the Arctic have changed remarkably in the past six years. As an indication of the government's current attitude, in 1959 a letter was sent to all government departments that have employees in the north, dealing with the question of relations with the indigenous population. There was no attempt whatever to curtail fraternization; indeed, the reverse is the case. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has a number of employees, both male and female, who are Eskimos married to white persons or white persons married to Eskimos. I might add that D.E.W. line

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all appreciate and commend the original intention in this particular clause contained in the D.E.W. line contract, which was primarily designed for the benefit of the Eskimo population itself. Whether or not the recommendation was unanimous, the responsibility is still that of the government. I take the position that it was not unanimous. If it is permissible I should like to make a brief reference to the joint ownership of Northern Alberta Railway company by the C.N.R. and C.P.R. In the loading and spotting of cars preference is given to Canadian Pacific rolling stock on the profitable runs while the less profitable runs, in terms of both distance and commodities carried, are given to the Canadian National. Undoubtedly this is done with the consent or knowledge of the board of directors of the C.N.R. The loading and spotting of cars are carried out in such a way that the Canadian National financial structure suffers while the Canadian Pacific financial structure benefits.

Would the hon. member permit a question? The statement he has just made strikes me as so extraordinary that I wish he would give us some evidence with respect to the basis for his statement so that the rest of us may assess it properly. On the face of it his statement seems impossible to believe, and if he has any evidence to support it I should like to hear it.

I will be glad to go into the matter further. I have here a reissue from Edmonton, dated March 7, 1961, of a circular dated December 1, 1960. There is a reference to file DT-914. The circular is addressed to all agents and there is the heading, "Ordering and spotting empty equipment". Perhaps I might read the part that is relevant to what we are discussing. First there is a reference to certain types of cars that are available, and then the circular goes on to say:
Cars of Canadian Pacific ownership must be loaded to competitive stations such as Vancouver, lakehead, Calgary, et cetera. Specify C.P. cars on your daily yard report.
This is one indication that Canadian Pacific cars must be loaded to competitive stations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not want the hon. member to go too far in this direction, because I do not see how he can relate what he is saying now to the increase in the number of directors.

That is why I simply made the general statement initially that this procedure obviously reflects the attitude of the directors, and it was only in answer to a question that I quoted part of the circular. I will be glad to make it available to the hon. member for Greenwood in order that he may read it at his leisure. The gist of the matter, and I think this is borne out by this circular issued
5158	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways Act by the Northern Alberta Railway, is that at the present time the C.N.R. board of directors undoubtedly takes the attitude that in a number of instances preference will be given to the Canadian Pacific while on less profitable runs preference will be given to the C.N.R. On the long, lucrative hauls Canadian Pacific cars are specified while on the short, nonlucrative hauls Canadian National cars are specified.
This, of course, is not an isolated instance. I think almost anyone having anything to do with either the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. will be able to cite additional circumstances which show substantially the same thing, that at the present time the Canadian National is not operated at peak efficiency. It does not engage in activities in which it should engage, and to a great extent I think this is the fault of the directors of the railroad.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not see how the hon. member can relate his remarks to the number of directors. I have indicated before that the present administration of the C.N.R. and the acts of the present directors are not relevant to the debate.

Certainly I do not want to run afoul of your rulings in any way, Mr. Chairman, but I thought I was on the correct course so far as the rules are concerned, or maybe I should say on the right track, because in my initial remarks I mentioned that the clause under consideration seeks to provide 12 directors for the C.N.R. I also pointed out that in the selection of these directors consideration should be given to choosing people who know the railroad business in order that the railway will be able to operate at the highest possible peak of efficiency. I submit it is not operating in that manner now primarily because of the background of the president of the railroad, who is also on the board of directors, and that of other officials as well.
I thought I was on the right track, Mr. Chairman. I mentioned that I had been allowed to make these remarks without anyone calling me to order-I am not casting any reflection upon yourself-and I assumed I could proceed along this line. I was saying this is the way the board of directors should be made up, and this is the type of representation there should be on the board of directors once this legislation is passed, in order to ensure that the things which I mentioned a while ago in connection with the Northern Alberta Railway do not occur again. We should ensure also that Canadian National Railways operates to the peak of efficiency and does not operate primarily to the advantage of the Canadian Pacific, as it has in some instances.


I think, Mr. Chairman, that in order to follow your ruling and your suggestion I should not make any additional remarks along that line, because I will obviously be called to order and I certainly do not want to run afoul of the rules of the house.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada

This, Mr. Chairman-

speechtext: I have not got the act in front of me, but I shall endeavour to find out.

While the minister is
checking the Canadian National Railways Act I should like to say a few words about clause 1, which proposes to increase the number of directors of Canadian National Railways from seven to 12. It is quite true that on May 15 and 16, during the discussion of the resolution related to this matter, I was absent from the house. I felt that some of the C.N.R. problems and some of the other major problems related to this country can only be decided if the shareholders of the C.N.R. and of this country on May 29 reach a favourable decision and indicate that they are not satisfied either with the C.N.R. or with some other matters related to our country.
Since returning to this chamber I have been asked about the statements I made when the committee on railways, air lines and shipping met last year, and how I reconciled the views I expressed on March 28 and 29, 1960 with those expressed by spokesmen of our party in the debate last week. I have
5160	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways Act no difficulty whatsoever in this respect, Mr. Chairman, when I refer to clause 1 of the bill before the committee.
When I advanced, as the hon. member for Vancouver South quoted me as saying, the suggestion that we might very well in the interests of the Canadian National Railways enlarge the board of directors, as reported at page 154 of the proceedings of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping, it will be found that I based my views on the belief that we could enlarge our board of directors for the purpose of having a larger crowd of boosters for the C.N.R. I was away last week, but when I read the debates that took place here I note that, as I would have expected, we do not find in the Conservative party boosters for the C.N.R. On the contrary, we find among their ranks those who always have something of ill will to say about the Canadian National Railways. In addition, as can be found at page 154 of the proceedings of the committee, in the remarks I made last year I stated:
There are many businessmen of great promise in private life who would consider a directorate in the C.N.R. a matter of compliment, honour and responsibility.
I also said that in the main the type of persons that I would seek to put on an enlarged board of the Canadian National Railways would be those associated with the provision of freight in large quantities for the Canadian National Railways. I advanced some examples with respect to the directorate of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
When I made those remarks in the committee last year, Mr. Chairman, I must confess that I had not looked carefully enough at the appointments that had been made by this present government since June, 1957 when they took office in Canada and up to the time of my remarks in the committee on March 28, 1960. I assumed that they were honour bound to place on the directorate of the Canadian National Railways those who would advance the interests of the Canadian National Railways first and foremost. I did not assume that they would appoint to the directorate of the C.N.R., which is not merely a multi-million dollar incorporation but a multi-billion dollar corporation, any persons other than those who were the best possible available in this country to advance the interests of the Canadian National Railways and ensure its success.
Since those remarks were made by me in the committee I confess that I have examined with more care the appointments that have been made by this government to the board of Canadian National Railways, and as a result I have some diffidence about saying by my vote "Me too", that I approve an


enlargement of the board through appointments of that type in the period that is ahead of us, the short period of time that might be available to this government before they lose office in which to make those appointments to the board of the Canadian National Railways.
I speak after some consideration and examination of the appointments that have been made to this board since 1957. For years and years since the Bennett government was in office, which government had no friendship for the Canadian National Railways, I assert, without any possible difficulty with respect to refutation that the Canadian National was given a directorate of citizens of this country, under the former Liberal administration, who would be beyond question likely to provide what I asked for in the committee last year, namely men who had connections with business people across this land and who were likely to provide freight, patronage, good will and prestige to the Canadian National Railways.
Since the advent of this government I assert that the Canadian National Railways has become a patronage vehicle. Indeed as the hon. member for Laurier asserted, it is related to unemployment because this might even be regarded as an unemployment measure. Defeated candidates of the Conservative party have been appointed to its board of directors. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggested that perhaps those who have some insecurity in the present situation might even be prospective candidates for this board in future. I observe the hon. member for Greenwood looking at me a bit askance.
Can you blame him?
Is the hon. member going to give us some facts to support this astounding statement?

Yes, I am going to give some facts to the hon. member for Greenwood. As I always do, I accorded him the courtesy of looking up his remarks, which are always greatly valued here in this chamber. I found that in my absence which I have admitted, the hon. member for Greenwood contributed to the debate at the resolution stage and made reference to one appointment and one appointment only. In referring to appointments to the C.N.R. board of directors made by the present administration he referred to the late Mr. E. W. Bickle, a businessman of great note and renown. As found at page 4851 of Hansard, the hon. member for Greenwood in referring to the calibre of directors that would be expected for this multi-billion dollar public enterprise stated as follows:

In my opinion the appointments that have been made are excellent. Mr. E. W. Bickle died regretted by everybody. I think he was a great asset to the railway.
I suggest to the hon. member that I have no quarrel there. Although I never met the late Mr. E. W. Bickle, I know something about his business connections. Even though he was national treasurer of the Conservative party, I do not hold the fact of appointment to the C.N.R. against him. He was an eminent businessman with widespread business connections which I think would be an asset to the Canadian National Railways. Then the hon. member for Greenwood-and I think this is where he is blind-went on to say this:
We have no reason to think that we will not get other men of the same calibre.
I just want the hon. member for Greenwood to look at the appointments that have already been made by the present Conservative government. There was a member of the board of directors representing the Atlantic provinces who had some connection with business in a way which I think would likely provide what I call freight to the Canadian National Railways. I am not going to mention his name, but he was replaced by a defeated Atlantic area Conservative candidate. I do not hold this against him, but I do not know very much about this gentleman because I cannot find his name in the Canadian "Who's Who''. His predecessor figured in that publication and was connected with many businesses; he was a man who could be expected to bring business to the C.N.R.
I find that in the provinces of western Canada which I know best a retired director of the C.N.R.-a man not referred to by the hon. member for Greenwood-who was the president of one of the largest grain shippers in western Canada was replaced by this government. As I say, this was not referred to by the hon. member for Greenwood when he mentioned a distinguished Canadian, Mr. E.	W. Bickle. This replacement to represent western Canada was a man who, according to "Who's Who", prior to his appointment was connected with an investment trust, a business which provides no freight. However, he is said in "Who's Who" to be the treasurer of the Conservative party in his province.
Which province is it?

It is the province of Saskatchewan. If one looks at the business connections of this affluent man one cannot find in "Who's Who" anything which could provide any traffic for the Canadian National Railways.
Canadian National Railways Act
When I made the statements I did in the committee last year it is clear I was suggesting an enlargement of the board to provide men of good will to the Canadian National Railways. I indicated I had even suggested this to my former chief, the present hon. member for Laurier. But my hon. friend from Laurier, as well as the former minister of transport, now Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Hees, had the opinion that I was wrong. I was expecting that appointments of this kind would not be of a nature which would provide a patronage vehicle-an unemployment measure in favour of defeated Progressive Conservative candidates-but that they would be made along the lines I suggested to the committee on railways, air lines and shipping not only last year but on earlier occasions.
I say that the C.N.R. has not been created to provide a prestige berth for treasurers and collectors for the Conservative party and defeated candidates. It was not established for the purpose of giving office and high prestige to tribute collectors. What we need is men of good will with good connections in business and industry. If I felt that this was implicit in the bill before us then I assure the government I would be prepared to support it in accordance with the observations I have previously made, but the record stands against them. I do not trust this government to make appointments, judging from the nature of the appointments they have made so far on a basis of about four to one.
On that basis I cannot support this proposal. What we have here is not a proposition to enlarge the board for the purpose of creating good will, an expansion of freight traffic and an improvement in the other business of the railway. I suggest the only kind of freight which will be provided by enlarging the board of this company is political freight, and they are running deadhead in the appointments which have been made so far, with perhaps one exception which the hon. member for Greenwood carefully selected, ignoring the others.
In the past western Canada had on this board of directors a man, now replaced, representing Canada's largest industry who was concerned with the carriage of grain by the railways of this country. I have indicated that in spite of this we have seen the appointment of an investment man who, regardless of his merit and personal qualifications, including those possessed by a collector for the Conservative party, is not, I suggest, representative of western Canada.
I notice that last week there was some discussion about the executive committee of the C.N.R. I had some experience of this in
5162	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways Act the past but I must say I did not realize, if it was always the case, that the executive committee is appointed by the president of the railway. I can tell all my colleagues in this house that if that is so I do not approve of it. I think the executive committee of the board of directors should be appointed by the vote of the board of directors, as is the case with the C.P.R.
I do want to say that this government has not replaced a farmer from western Canada by a farmer. In the former executive committee of the Canadian National Railways, as I remember it, there was among this small group a representative of labour. He happened to be a personal friend of mine-
Oh, oh.

He was no political friend of mine; I know nothing about his politics. I am thinking of my boyhood on the prairies at the age of 12 and of my knowing at that time a certain member of the railway running trades working out of the C.N.R. Dauphin terminal. He was a man who rose to become a distingushed labour director of the C.N.R. Mr. Daly. 1 only met him once after I had matured, but he was a representative of the labour force on that executive committee and for a long time he was a resident of the city of Dauphin, as I was. However, as I say, in later years he was a member of the executive committee and I think he held that office for more than ten years. The former minister of transport, my colleague the hon. member for Laurier, knows more about that than I do.
What I wish to say is this. Where is the representative of labour now on the C.N.R. executive committee? In our committee last year a question was raised which I feel should receive some amplification. That was the propriety, if it happened, of a former member of this house taking a position on the directorate of either of these big railways.
At page 153 of the proceedings of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping I made reference to an individual who I think certainly was the father of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and who has provided great qualities of leadership to Canadian National Railways. I refer, of course, to the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe. One of the greatest tributes that can be paid to the Canadian National Railways, with reference to the late Mr. Howe, is found in the calibre of man he suggested, when he was the minister, should be appointed to the board of directors of Canadian National Railways. I am sure the influence of his suggestions prevailed on his successor, as minister of transport, in so far as the calibre of man required was concerned.


I find nothing in the appointments that were made by Mr. Howe or his successor that would indicate that the Canadian National Railways have become the tool of a political organization or party, and I feel it is unfair to make such a suggestion in respect of that person who was champion of the Canadian National Railways for such a long period of time.
Perhaps the statement was made because of the lack of facts, however, as indicated at page 153 of the proceedings of the railways, air lines and shipping committee. The present member for Port Arthur, a man described as a learned reader and perhaps a giant in that field, as reported on page 153 of the committee:
I have gone through the C.P.R. annual report, and I find in reading that report that Mr. Crump is not the only one who speaks to the shareholders. As a matter of fact, I have seen records where Mr. C. D. Howe has spoken to the shareholders, and a certain number of the directors make comments. This is the sort of thing I thought might be possible with the C.N.R.
Then I said at that point, as reported on the same page:
Is Mr. Howe a director of the C.P.R.?
Mr. Chairman, I rose at that point because I knew that Mr. Howe, having been so long the champion of efficiency and advance for the Canadian National Railways was not likely to very popular with the C.P.R. directorship. The hon. member for Port Arthur then is reported as having said "yes", followed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, as follows:
Have you lost track of what he is doing now?

Yes, in this respect, even if he was my near ex-neighbour in a northern Ontario riding.
I have checked the annual reports of the Canadian Pacific Railway-

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member if he heard the apology I made both in the committee and in the house relative to this statement, and the explanation I gave; that I had confused the report of the Bank of Montreal and the annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway? I cannot see the relevancy of his remark if he heard that apology and explanation.

Mr. Chairman, I confess that I had not heard that explanation, or seen it. If I had, I should not have raised this subject. My colleague the hon. member for Essex East assures me that such an apology and explanation was made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, and I accept that immediately as being so. I assure that hon. member that I would not have raised this argument had I been aware of the circumstances.

Today we have this blossoming forth of vice presidents, executives and officers of the C.N.R. in a fashion that was not contemplated by the committee last year. If we were to rely upon the rosy prospects as presented to us by the Minister of Finance last year, we should not have expected the unemployment situation that presently exists. The hon. member for Laurier was perfectly relevant in saying there is tremendous resentment across this country today because of the fact that we are now enlarging the board of directors. The existing board of directors, as now constituted, have approved the enlargement of management, in respect of vice presidents, to a much greater number than is available to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Now is not the time to provide employment to defeated candidates and treasurers and others of the Conservative party. On the contrary, this parliament must insist that the management of these railways be checked very carefully because of the tremendous obligations, in respect of maintenance and employment, with which we are involved, as well as because of the effects this has on our national economy. I think the employees of the Canadian National Railways would be the first to admit that the time they are going to be hurt, in so far as lay-offs are concerned, will be this time when the C.N.R. is in poor shape so far as its balance sheet is concerned, and in so far as its income and outgo are concerned. That is the time when job slaughtering occurs.
I suggest the government should give management confidence, but at the moment even the president is not aware of his position. I do not advocate that he be reappointed, but I do suggest that what is lacking, as in every other sphere of operation in connection with government, is leadership and decisiveness. This is a multi-billion dollar corporation, but the government stands idle in its policy so that even the C.N.R. president does not know whether he is going to last until next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have witnessed this afternoon a perfect example of a political somersault. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has our sympathy in this regard, because he was in a very tough spot. There can be no doubt that he has been a great advocate of increasing the number of directors of the Canadian National Railways. He was not here last week when we discussed this bill, but he now comes into the committee with his dream of the last few days, which I doubt very much if anyone will bite on. When the hon. member appeared in the sessional committee last year he knew that every person he has named this afternoon had been
Canadian National Railways Act a director of the C.N.R. for at least two years; but all of a sudden, in the last few days, he has found out that fact.
In 1959, almost a year before that committee's hearings, the hon. member made a very forceful and excellent argument in favour of increasing the membership of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. He made another forceful speech in this house on June 15, 1959, at which time he presented exactly the same viewpoint he has presented this afternoon. I should like to ask him now, Mr. Chairman, through you, to inform us at which time he was expressing his true opinion; is it today, or was it when he appeared in the sessional committee?
This afternoon he suggests that the government intends to use the board of directors of the C.N.R. as a political tool. I should like to inform him that this government has appointed some very excellent public servants to that board of directors, and will continue to do so. As I have said earlier, the government intends that directors on the board of the Canadian National Railways shall be first Canadians; second, good businessmen; and finally, individuals who have at heart the good of this country as well as the welfare of the Canadian National Railways, on which board they have been appointed.

Let us carefully analyse the appointments made by the new government since it assumed office. Will the minister deny that Mr. Bickle was national treasurer of the Conservative party? Will he deny that the second director happened to be a defeated Conservative candidate? Will he deny that the third director happened to be the treasurer of the Conservative party in a province? Will he deny that the labour representative was a reappointment which could not be abused but he had been appointed by the previous government?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: To show precisely that we are not playing politics in those appointments, may I say we did not hesitate to reappoint Hon. Wilfrid Gagnon, who had exactly the same position as far as the Liberal party is concerned as Mr. Bickle had in the Conservative party.

I have been somewhat interested in the remarks made this afternoon regarding increasing the number of directors of the C.N.R. from seven to 12. As some hon. members may know, Alberta has not been favoured with a representative on the board. Alberta is one of those provinces which have been very greatly concerned over railroading and railroading problems over the years. I heartily support the proposed legislation to increase the number of directors of the C.N.R. mainly because when
5164	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways Act that is done all provinces will perhaps be truly represented on the board of directors, and the members of the board will then be able to bring to the attention of the management of the C.N.R. problems concerning their various provinces.
In the 1960 railway committee the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated the reasons why he thought the number on the board of directors should be increased. I agree with him in so far as the reasons are concerned. One of the reasons was that a large group could keep in touch with potential suppliers of business. This is certainly true. The hon. member went on to point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway had something like 25 directors on its board. There is quite a marked difference between seven and 25.
If the whole reason for increasing the number from seven to 12 was patronage, I do not know why the government would stop at 12. Why not make it 25 and give that many more jobs? I do not think that is the reason. The reason is to bring about a higher degree of efficiency in management with the least cost, and to give representation to all parts of Canada.
In the 1960 committee reports at page 154, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River went on to say that governments in the past as well as now have been missing the boat. Those were the words he used, and he suggested the number should be increased.
Not by appointment of political friends.
Don't be so self-righteous.

We will deal with political friends in a minute. The hon. member went on to say:
I think the directorate in the C.N.R. is too small in number, that it puts too much responsibility on management, and is not developing freight in the way that the rival company is.
This is the very point. The men appointed to the board of directors should be those with a particular knowledge of railroading and how it affects various parts of Canada, so they might aid the C.N.R. in developing business and freight, and who are in touch with potential suppliers of business.
We had a great deal of discussion in the committee this morning with regard to this subject and I do not intend to belabour it, other than to say I was interested in the point of view of the official Liberal party and in the fact that in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate he suggested the present chairman of the board of directors should be reappointed. Furthermore, there is nothing wrong in the members of a government, when it comes to making an appointment favourably, considering those among their friends who deserve a reward for certain services, and especially for their marked contribution to the affairs of the country.
Mr. Chairman, I find it is rather strange that hon. members opposite should rise in protest against what they call political patronage. Can they really take the floor, one after the other, to say seriously that the leaders of the Liberal party of years past, and especially those of the previous governments have never considered, when an appointment had to be made, in the C.N.R. or elsewhere, the services of their friends?

Can the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill), who was on very intimate terms with the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, tell us seriously that his famous master never considered the political viewpoint when making appointments? Can those gentlemen tell us that Mr. St. Laurent has always ignored political considerations, when it was a case of appointing someone to a certain position? Can those hon. members opposite tell us with a straight face that they have never tried to reward the political services of some of their friends through appointments? Do the hon. members opposite really have the gall to tell the house they have never considered the services of their supporters in their 22 years of administration? Can they really say they have ignored those services, and have really chosen at random, or in other parties, the men they wanted to appoint to any office? I do not believe it, Mr. Chairman.
I do not believe our friends opposite, and particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who I see is smiling, could say that political considerations were always very far from the mind of the Hon. Mackenzie King. In fact, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is one of the biographers of Mr. King, recognizes in his book the political acumen of his former master. I really believe, Mr. Chairman, that the present discussion is not serious, and I shall go as far as to say that it is in rather poor taste for the members opposite to accuse the present government of a mistake, if indeed it is one, that they themselves made repeatedly during the 22 years they were in office, namely from 1935 to 1957.
I also fail to understand why our friends opposite persist in saying that the present government is showing indecision and lack of leadership by asking the house to increase the membership of the C.N.R. board of directors. On the contrary, I feel this is a measure showing determination and a progressive spirit, because the present government realizing the importance of railways in our country and admitting that the C.N.R. constitute a fiscal burden for the treasury, that demands the attention of the best minds in the country, acknowledges the fact that, in view of the importance of the C.N.R. services, an increased number of directors should be entrusted with the care of looking into its
Canadian National Railways Act operations. Therefore, the government feels it is essential to help the C.N.R. administration by increasing the membership of its board of directors.
I cannot find any evidence of lack of leadership or any trace of indecision in this legislation. Quite the contrary, I feel that it indicates real decision, and if there is any indecision and confusion, it is in the minds of my hon. friends opposite who are trying to play politics with this question, which in my opinion should be foreign to politics.

This government which came into power hardly four years ago, has already made four political appointments to the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways, which has only seven members. I have here the reports of the Canadian National Railways, and would like the Associate Minister of National Defence, or the Minister of Transport to tell us where, with perhaps one exception, there have been political appointments, in the true sense of the word, to the board of directors of the Canadian National when we were in power.
We tried not to let party politics interfere with the administration of the Canadian National Railways. I said so the other night, and I repeat today, that if we want to destroy the management of the Canadian National, let us introduce politics into it. I would not say
[The Chairman.]
that this government means to do that, but the appointment of four out of the seven present directors were political or nearly political appointments. The best proof is that in 1957 the Hon. Wilfrid Gagnon was reappointed to the board of directors of the C.N.R.
The Hon. Wilfrid Gagnon is a personal friend of mine, a man of great distinction whose stamp on the affairs of Quebec and Canada has been impressive. There is no sin in that.

Hopeless behaviour of this kind is inexcusable in connection with an organization, which, as my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River has reminded us is a multi-billion dollar corporation costing the Canadian taxpayer millions of dollars a year, though this was not the case a few years ago when we had a different administration. speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-98, to amend the Canada Shipping Act.
Canada Shipping Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think the bill we have before us at the present time is an important one even if it contains more detail and minor amendments. It might not have the importance of the previous bill, according to my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate, but I still recommend it to the house.
The Canada Shipping Act is a very lengthy document which deals with virtually all aspects involving technical regulation and administration of matters relating to shipping. Since it deals with these matters in considerable detail, it is not surprising that, from time to time, some of its clauses become out of date and require amendment or amplification. This can happen because of technical changes in the marine field, because of changes in international law and agreements, and because of changes in the laws of other countries. It can happen also because of changes in the status of various areas affected.
A statute such as this has to be brought up to date from time to time and the amendments contained in the present bill are amendments which we have been collecting for a period of four or five years for this purpose, rather than seeking to introduce amendments of this sort at virtually every session.
Because the changes are technical in nature and are numerous, I do not intend to describe every one of them in this speech. Since I propose to refer the bill to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, there will be ample opportunity at that time to go into each clause in detail. Any general review on my part at this time might overlook points or clauses which some hon. members may consider important, but I will at least attempt to mention a few of the more important changes in broad terms.
The present bill contains revised definitions of home-trade voyage, inland waters and minor waters. There is at present an anomaly in the definition of home-trade voyage in that a Canadian vessel can, in theory, make an extended voyage as a home-trade ship around the whole North American continent with the exception of a comparatively short portion betweeen the north end of the Bering strait and cape Spencer in Alaska. If, however, the Canadian ship goes from Prince Rupert through the Bering strait to a Canadian port in the Canadian western Arctic, she is considered a foreign-going ship. The amendment provides for the classification of a voyage through this area as a home-trade voyage, which is consistent with our definition elsewhere; and it also brings the wording of this section up to date in view of the fact that Alaska and Hawaii are now states in the United States of America. The addition

Canada Shipping Act
of Newfoundland, including Labrador, as an additional province of Canada, will also now be covered under the clause.
The definition of inland waters will be changed by the bill to include the port of Havre St. Pierre, about 50 miles east of the present limits in this definition. This will be of assistance to our lake ships making voyages to the gulf of St. Lawrence, and to our coastal traffic on the St. Lawrence. To avoid any misunderstanding, however, I should add that this is not related to the proposal which I announced recently to limit our domestic coasting trade in the great lakes area to vessels of Canadian registry. The necessary amendment for that purpose is not included in the present bill since we have not yet concluded our diplomatic consultations. However, while it is not exactly relevant to this bill, I might tell the house that I will have a correction to make in the announcement I made the other day as far as the limit downriver is concerned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Instead of Les Escoumains.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Instead of Les Escoumains it will be inland waters and the limit will be as mentioned here. I should like to add that the Canada Shipping Act will not be changed at the present time to cover any of the matters dealt with in the announcement I made the other day. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
That is right. This will be in the note that we will send to the other countries of the commonwealth who have signed the commonwealth shipping agreement.
The definition of minor waters in Canada has been amended to include lake Winnipeg to assist ship operators on that lake who, up to the present, have been required to have the same degree of certification as ships on the great lakes where conditions are quite different. The amendment will place lake Winnipeg in the same class as other bodies of water in the Canadian west such as lake Manitoba, lake Athabaska and Great Slave lake.
We also propose to correct an anomaly existing with regard to the position of bodies corporate from the Republic of Ireland in the matter of ship registry. At present an

Irish citizen may qualify to be the owner of a British ship but a company incorporated under Irish law does not have this privilege. This arises because of the effect on Canadian law of certain changes made in both United Kingdom and Irish law over recent years.
In recognition of the substantial growth of pleasure boating in Canada, we propose to adjust the tonnage floor with regard to registration of pleasure yachts. At present any pleasure craft over 15 tons must be registered while any craft under 15 tons need only be licensed under the simpler small craft procedure, although it may be registered if the owner desires. We propose to raise the 15 tons to 20 tons so that the simpler procedure of licensing may in future be followed by those owners of pleasure craft between 15 and 20 tons.
There are quite extensive changes and adjustments made with regard to the requirement for engineering personnel on ships. I will not attempt to describe these in detail but will only mention one or two examples. We are providing for the first time for a special certificate for the chief engineers of motor-driven fishing vessels who up to the present have been required to hold a third-class engineering certificate. The examination for the new proposed certificate will be based primarily on practical knowledge. We believe this will be of considerable help to the fishing industry.
On the other hand, we are providing that on large home-trade, inland and minor waters ships a first class engineer be carried while previously the maximum requirement was for a second class engineer. We believe this is a necessary step in the direction of safety due to the larger, more powerful and more complicated types of machinery being used. The rights of engineers who obtained certificates of competency for this purpose prior to the passage of this new legislation will, nevertheless, be recognized.
Also, in view of strong representations received from our coastal tug boat operators, we propose that tugs of not more than 150 tons gross tonnage, where full control may be exercised from the bridge, may be exempt from the carriage of certificated engineers when making voyages of the inland or home-trade type. All of these and the other proposed amendments of this type have been very carefully examined by our steamship inspection service to satisfy ourselves that we are in no way affecting the necessary degree of safety in operations.
We also recognize that there may be special cases where it is unnecessary to require a deck officer of a ferry vessel to have a broad marine certificate and that the prime requisite need be only expert knowledge of the

ferry run itself, and we are providing that special certificates may be issued for this purpose.
There is also a clause which provides for adjustment in regard to exemptions from compulsory pilotage dues in one pilotage district only, namely, between Cornwall and Montreal. To place this district on the same basis as other pilotage districts farther down the river, introduction of compulsory pilotage dues has been desirable. However, in order to accord fair and equal treatment to United States vessels in this connection, it is necessary to introduce an amendment to permit exemption of United States vessels along with the present exemptions accorded to Canadian and British vessels. The highly co-operative attitude of the United States in working out joint pilotage arrangements on the great lakes justifies a modification of this sort. This has been discussed fully with and explained to the pilots.
In the field of small pleasure craft, which is becoming increasingly active, we have decided that as a result of experience we should extend our authority to maintain necessary safety measures somewhat. At present we have the authority to require specified safety equipment to be carried in powered vessels but, as a result of lengthy study and discussion, we have decided that the time has come when we should seek authority also to establish regulations regarding safety equipment, that is, lifejackets, et cetera, which should be carried in unpropelled vessels at present outside the scope of the act. Similarly, as a result of experience we propose to provide for the compulsory marking of small pleasure vessels with some sort of plating which will show the safe limitation of engine horsepower and gross load capacity for that particular type of boat. This has been tried out on a voluntary basis over the last couple of years and has been very successful.
We have a clause which will strengthen our machinery with regard to marine search and rescue by granting additional powers to marine search and rescue co-ordinators when engaged in marine search and rescue activities.
We also have certain clauses changing the present provisions about limitation of liability. The changes will give effect to provisions of the international convention relating to the limitation of liability of owners of sea-going ships, signed at Brussels on October 10, 1957. Here again, the full explanation would be complicated, but one principal effect will be to adjust upwards substantially the old limitations of liability which have not been changed for many years. Owners' liability where there are both property and personal claims is being raised from $72.97 per ton to 3,100 gold francs 90205-6-328

$206, and in respect of property claims only from $38.92 to 1,000 gold francs or $65.
The definition of "ship" is slightly broadened as is the coverage of the clauses generally. Recognition also is given to the paramount position of national law in overriding these limitations where applicable.
As I indicated at the beginning of these remarks, a full description of all the clauses in the bill would probably take another hour or two. I trust, however, that for the purposes of this debate and in view of my intention to refer the bill to the standing committee, members of the house will find this present explanation satisfactory.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to make a long speech on the bill at this time. I think it is understandable that from time to time it is necessary to amend an act of such proportions as the Canada Shipping Act in order to meet various changes and modern demands and practice. The present bill is one that contains 41 clauses, some of which are of a minor nature while others will need detailed study. I believe, therefore, this is the type of bill that could be more properly handled in a committee than in the house and I was very pleased to hear the minister say it will be sent to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I believe this procedure would give members an opportunity to get a very clear explanation of the different provisions in the bill.
I am particularly interested in some of the provisions such as those relating to fishing boats. I notice that the bill, when referring to fishing boats, refers to the fact that certain boats must have engineers with certificates if the boats have a power beyond a certain nominal horsepower. For the purposes of clarification, I should like to have horsepower stated in terms other than nominal because I think they would be more easily understood by the fishermen who will be guided by the terms of this bill.
I note, too, that the minister made reference to the fact there are some clauses in the bill dealing with pilotage. I would think that pilotage is becoming more important all the time, particularly in view of the announcement by the minister of a new shipping policy and because of the St. Lawrence seaway. Pilotage is important to me because I think we have some places in Newfoundland where pilotage could be better implemented than it is at the moment. I am referring to the port of Corner Brook on the west coast of Newfoundland, and on some other occasion I shall have an opportunity of referring to that matter more fully than a discussion of this measure will permit.

Canada Shipping Act
I feel that the provisions dealing with the safety of pleasure craft are of great importance and should be well discussed in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. There is nothing more I want to say in connection with this bill, Mr. Speaker. As I said at the outset of these remarks, I feel this is the type of measure that can be more properly discussed in a committee and when that time comes we will be prepared to take up the different items in the committee.

The Canada Shipping Act is a truly important piece of legislation. In my opinion, it is a basic part of our legislation dealing with one of our most important industries. In past years, there has been a decreasing amount of shipping done by our own Canadian ships. Our Canadian fleet has decreased year by year. This has been due to many factors, and I am sure all hon. members hope that the amendments now being brought forward in this particular bill will help to promote and facilitate shipping in our Canadian waters.
The bill, as was explained by the minister, covers a great number of amendments, some of which are of an important nature while others are of minor significance. I hope that it will be possible, when the bill is returned to the committee of the whole, for Canadian shipping to be discussed fully with a view to extending all possible facilities to this extremely important Canadian industry.
I do not have to mention to the house that our country is largely a trading country and it is at times disconcerting to see ships other than Canadian ships travelling along our rivers and lakes, and all our products being moved in bottoms other than Canadian bottoms. I feel that this whole shipping problem might well be discussed during the study of this particular bill. I cannot at this moment say what the effects of the proposed changes will be. Once we are in committee, it will be easier to study each of the clauses in detail.
There are included in the bill, as my hon. friend said a while ago, provisions relating to fishing vessels as well as the registry of ships, the definition of "ships" and "inland waters", all of which are of tremendous importance in determining just how beneficial to Canadian ship owners these amendments might be.
There is one amendment in particular to which I should like to refer directly and that has to do with pleasure craft. I am happy to see that the government has taken some steps to regulate the movement of pleasure craft. I am quite sure all hon. members realize that this particular activity is becoming an important industry in our country and that our 
rivers and lakes are filled with craft of all types. There seems to be a growing tendency to increase the horsepower of motors, while at the same time to decrease the sturdiness and weight of the hull in order to get greater speed. Although like everyone else I like to have great speed, I believe it would be wise to make sure that it is not overdone and that we do not incur dangers which could easily be avoided by regulation. There are, as hon. members know, a considerable number of accidents each year with these craft with huge motors and hardly any hull. It may be that, with the help of the regulations, we can avoid these lamentable accidents and, at the same time, not destroy the pleasure that can be derived from these craft. I hope it will be my pleasure, during the time the bill comes before the committee, to ask all the questions that arise in connection with each one of the clauses of this bill. I hope that eventually the effect of the bill, once it passes, will be to help Canadian ships in our own waters.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly on this bill at this time. It is a very important measure. It is not a spectacular type of bill or one likely to arouse the same, shall I say, debate as that which we experienced on the previous measure. It has to do more with things than with human beings in one respect, or the operating of things rather than the action of human beings which was under discussion when we were dealing with the directors of the C.N.R.
On second reading of a bill we are supposed to discuss the principle of it. However, I find it extremely difficult indeed to decide what is the principle of a bill like this one. It is a bill of 41 sections. They are technical in some respects; they are interesting to me in other respects. But how you, Mr. Speaker, would decide whether or not I was departing from the principle of the bill, is more than I can understand or foresee. However, I trust that you, in your wisdom, will bring me back to the right course if I should go off on the wrong compass lead. I suppose one can only say that the principle of this bill is to provide for greater safety at sea in the operation of ships of all kinds and for more efficient administration of the shipping industry as applied to the Canada Shipping Act and its regulations.
We have not had this interesting measure in our hands for very long. In view of our many other duties under these circumstances, I am quite sure most of the members have not had the opportunity to study the sections of the bill. On briefly glancing over the measure I was particularly interested in the sections that applied to pleasure craft, as was

one of the other hon. members who spoke. I think some amendments are necessary with respect to the control of pleasure craft. They are increasing in numbers in our inland and minor waters and there is need for a greater degree of control for the safety of the public.
I was also interested in the section which deals with tugs and small vessels used in the fishing industry. There again, what a different situation we face today from that which existed a few years ago. As far as tugs are concerned in the minor inland waters of British Columbia, years ago you would find them powered by steam and much larger in size than they are at the present time. Now they are on the whole powered by diesel engines. Their hulls and their structure are smaller in size than that required for vessels powered by steam and at the same time they have much greater power. These changing conditions with respect to hull types and power-and I am speaking particularly of tugs-certainly necessitates some change in the regulations and in the act.
The same thing applies to the fishing industry in which I presume conditions have been changing. However, I have not the same direct knowledge of that aspect of the matter. Most of my fishing is done from a launch casting a fly and that sort of thing. I know that some of my friends to my left wish to speak. I know that one of my colleagues from Newfoundland is bursting to get to his feet and say something about fishing, while at the same time hoping that I will not stop too soon. I am sure he is very well informed. The members from the maritime provinces will also have a contribution to make to this debate.

Our traditions are largely maritime traditions and our long coastline, east, west and north, together with our great inland waterways make shipping of vital importance to all of us. Our fortunes depend in the final analysis on seaborne trade, and it has been thus ever since Canada began to be a nation.
The first settlers arrived by ship and depended upon ships for their supplies. The inland waterways became highways for exploration and arteries of trade. Today, although rail and air transportation are an essential means of moving people and goods it is ocean borne commerce which remains, nevertheless, the final arbiter of Canada's wealth.
Laws and regulations to govern the movement of ships have existed for many years and, like all laws, must be amended from time to time to keep abreast of events. The Canada Shipping Act is no exception. It is an important piece of legislation and it must be

What is Tonnage
How often when speaking about a ship does someone ask "What tonnage is she"-and how seldom is the reply really completely understood!
"Tonnage'' does not always imply "weight"-it sometimes means "capacity".
There are four principal ways of describing the tonnage of any ship and brief descriptions of these methods follow:
Displacement is the tonnage used to describe all warships-it represents the total weight in tons of all the ship and its contents-it is called "displacement" because it is based upon the Archimedean principle that a floating body displaces an amount of water which is the same weight as the body itself.
Deadweight is the tonnage commonly used to describe the size of cargo ships-it represents the total carrying capacity of the ship in tons, including cargo, fuel, fresh water, stores, etc.
Gross registered tonnage is the tonnage usually used to describe passenger vessels-it represents the total internal cubic capacity of the ship, including accommodation spaces, each 100 cubic feet of which is "one ton" (ton of capacity).

This method of measurement goes back to the days when the size of a ship was judged by the number of barrels or "tuns" of wine it could carry-"tunnage" has now become "tonnage".
Gross tonnage is used as a basis for many marine rules and regulations and for assessing drydock dues, etc. It is also used for assessing St. Lawrence Seaway ship tolls (in addition to the ship toll, there is a toll on actual cargo carried).
Net registered tonnage is the gross tonnage minus certain deductible spaces which do not produce revenue, principally spaces occupied by crew, propelling machinery and fuel.
It is intended to be an indication of the earning capacity of a ship and as such is often used as a basis for canal tolls, harbour dues, dockage fees, etc.
An indication of the wide variety of "tonnages" which can apply to any ship is readily understood from the following figures, each of which relates to a typical 10,000 ton deadweight cargo vessel:
Displacement tonnage	 14,000
Deadweight tonnage	 10,000
Gross tonnage	 7,000
Net tonnage	 4,800
Newsletter No. 4	April, 1961
Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association Ottawa, Canada

the safety of life at sea, with wrecks and salvage, with public harbours, port wardens, limitation of liabilities, the coasting trade, delivery of goods, legal proceedings and, as I said, the international load line and the safety of life at sea.
It is unfortunate that various ministers, including those of the previous administration as well as those of the present administration, have seen fit to introduce substantial amendments to this act from time to time. These are amendments that have to be made, of course, but I say it is unfortunate in this sense. While I occupied the position now held by the minister I believe I brought in three amending bills and my successor, the Hon. Mr. Marler brought in one, if not more. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the various speeches made by members on this A.R.D.A. bill have added considerably, I believe, to the general knowledge of the purposes and principles of this legislation across the country. I do not know how many members spoke on this measure, but I do know from a reading of the press across Canada that there has been a considerable interest in each of the localities whose member put forward their point of view in connection with this bill.
I was particularly pleased when the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) mentioned the contribution of the late Dr. Blair from Lanark because if someone had not mentioned his contribution I had intended to do so. In my last remarks to the house, I mentioned that one of my purposes in delaying the passage of the bill until the month of May was to give me an opportunity to discuss, formally and informally with the provinces and farm organizations, the various points of view with regard to the proposed legislation and the various types of activity that could be carried out under its terms.
I am now able to report to the house that I have had formal consultations with eight of the provincial governments and several farm organizations, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The sum total of these discussions, in broad outline, is that the organizations believe, in the main, the terms of the bill are broad enough to cover the various ideas they have in mind. Some of the organizations did discuss slight amendments, but after discussion agreed that the
5194	HOUSE OF
Marginal Lands Development terms of the bill were broad enough to cover the purposes that they had included in their representations.
I also discussed with the provinces several steps that could be taken in each of their areas to raise farm income and give increased opportunity to the farmers in their respective provinces. We discussed with the provinces several types of programs that might apply not only within their provinces but across several provinces. I think it is well to report that in most cases the various departments affected in each of the provinces have in many cases gone ahead with their plans even before the bill has become statutory law. They recognize the importance of this legislation to that segment of the farm population which has been overlooked in the legislation affecting agriculture in the years gone by.
I also discussed with the provinces several facts and I have consulted with several of the academic leaders of our country, the deans of agriculture of several of our leading agricultural colleges, and have outlined to them the purposes of the bill and asked if they would submit ideas to me. Some of them have been very good in sending in lists of ideas and, together with the ideas, a statement concerning the principle that should be followed in the implementation of the bill.
Before I go into the principle of the bill I think I should take a few minutes in which to answer some of the statements made in the house in condemnation of the bill. The particular remarks to which I refer were made by the leader of the C.C.F. party. His comments were made on the second reading of the bill when he spoke a week ago Saturday. He said that the bill does not state what the act will do. He also said it does not say what the financial contributions will be. This is true, Mr. Speaker, because no one in the provinces or in the farm organizations or at the federal level knows yet what the bill will bring forth and the extent to which we are going to use this bill. The thing that has impressed me is the tremendous variety of ideas that have been put forward by the provincial ministers and by farm organizations of the things that they think are worth while and would benefit not only particular areas but the whole country.
Another point made by the hon. member for Assiniboia was that he was not so confident that the government would push this legislation forward. In a derogatory way he referred to previous legislation passed by this government and said there was a great fanfare and that nothing was done. I should like to remind the house that this particular bill is part of a national agricultural policy which was announced in the house on August


30, 1958. The hon. member for Assiniboia said that this bill was a deathbed repentance of the government, or words to that effect, and that we were duplicating the example of the P.F.R.A. legislation in 1935, bringing it in at the last minute. I should like to remind the members of the house that this particular bill was announced as one of the points of the national agricultural program on August 30, 1958; that the government has systematically each year brought in legislation under that program, and that this is just one part of that total program. This type of criticism in the face of the general acceptance of this legislation across the whole country and in the face of the enthusiastic reaction to this bill by leaders in farm thought who for generations have tried to get governments to accept something along this line I think disposes very quickly of the argument of the hon. member for Assiniboia.
A great deal of to-do was raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia about the pamphlet which was published by the department as part of the explanatory program to farm organizations and to the various provincial ministers. I think what has been overlooked in the description of this pamphlet as being an insult to parliament is this. If you look at the wording of item No. 4 in the orders of the day, you will find it reads in this way:
Resuming debate on the motion of the Minister of Agriculture for the second reading of Bill C-77, an act to provide for the rehabilitation of agricultural lands and the development of rural areas in Canada.
I think the whole argument collapses on the simple ground that this pamphlet about which there has been so much discussion uses the word "act" as it is used in the order paper and therefore is absolutely correct parliamentary usage. If hon. members look at the pamphlet, as I know they all have done, they will note that it states:
On December 15, 1960, the Minister of Agriculture introduced to the House of Commons a resolution concerned with improving the economic position of our farmers. The resolution introduces the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act (A.R.D.A. for short). This legislation will enable the government to enter into agreements-
The future tense is used throughout. The point that I have made is that by every definition, legal and common sense, this pamphlet is correct. It was a very essential part in the education of the public with regard to what this bill could do for Canada because, without the full and enthusiastic support not only of governments but of farm organizations, as well as of business people and professional people in this country, there would be no purpose in going ahead with

this bill. Essentially, it is based on the premise that there will be co-operation between all these groups.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as to the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, he said this act should be entitled an act to replace the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. He then went on to take to his bosom the Liberal party and said that they had done so much for conservation. As he made that speech we in the house all thought that he was assuming that the present leader of the Liberal party was not going to remain their leader forever; and that he was assuming that if he lost out with the New party candidature he would be in a position to move right into the soon to be vacated leadership of the Liberal party.
