speechtext: Shame.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS RESPECTING MARGINAL LANDS, RURAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Therefore, in conclusion, having regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia, I should just like to compare what he said on the resolution stage with what he said on second reading. I remember the thunder rolling through this house on the resolution stage when he said this bill was no good; that it was a sideshow with which to amuse the public; that what this government should do is face up to the fundamental facts facing agriculture and that the fundamental facts facing agriculture were the sale of wheat. As reported at page 1414 of Hansard he said this:
The minister said he was going to raise his sights with respect to getting markets for Canadian wheat. When he did so he got his sights up to a mark 20 million bushels lower than the accomplishment of the former minister of trade and commerce. This inability of the Minister of Agriculture to dispose of the surplus agricultural commodities in the world today condemns the government's over-all agricultural policy.
That was on January 25, 1961. The hon. member condemned this bill because it did not do anything to sell agricultural products and said that the government's agricultural policy had failed completely because we had not sold wheat. Later he came back to the house. He had been visiting out west. I do not know what kind of terror ran up his spine, but when he heard the comments of the farmers and when he read the editorials in the western press-Liberal, Social Credit and C.C.F.-and when he heard the remarks of the farm leaders, he raced back to Ottawa in order to try to cast doubt on the fact that we had sold a quantity of grain. He therefore, had to make up a new speech for second reading. What he said this time was that the bill was no good because it was going to abolish P.F.R.A.
This bill in its third set of principles is simply applying to all Canada the principles
Marginal Lands Development of P.F.R.A. How long have the members from British Columbia asked in this house for some form of physical rehabilitation to the river valleys, land that has to be drained, land that has to be dammed up to give water to land which could become fertile where producers are in mortal competition with those who are using water for irrigation to the south of the line and with whom the British Columbia farmer has been unable to compete fairly? How long have we heard the people of the maritimes asking for something broader than the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act? Anyone who drives through the Atlantic areas of this country and sees area after area which could be brought up to new levels of prosperity, thereby adding to farm income and community life by a simple application of the a.b.c.'s of the use of water will realize how necessary this new bill is.
I might mention in passing that we do have the Canada Water Conservation Act. This act was passed in 1953, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was careful to point out the other day in the house. What he did not point out was how many areas, how many provinces, have used this legislation which was passed in 1953. If one compares the amount of use of the Canada Water Conservation Act of 1953, making a comparison between the years 1953-1957 and 19571961 he will soon recognize that this was almost empty legislation as far as the Liberals were concerned. The first government to make real use of this legislation was the present administration. The tragedy is that the only province which has used it to date is the province of Ontario. Now we have legislation based on different principles, including the principles of the Canada Water Conservation Act, which will apply to all parts of Canada and at long last the unity of this country has moved a step forward in the conservation field because we are making one law for all Canadians and not one law for just part of Canada.
I hope in the days ahead to have fruitful discussions with the provincial ministers of every province in this country to lay down, I hope in this year 1961, a minimum of at least one tentative agreement in each province for at least one pilot area and, I hope, several in each province. The preliminary discussions I have had with the four western ministers indicate they have a list of projects they would like to put forward. Some of them have already been mentioned but others will be new to the members of the house.
I should like to mention in passing that the idea, the philosophy of this new act, is to build up income and not to push farmers off the land. An example of the type of thinking you have in the House of
5196	HOUSE OF
Marginal Lands Development Commons sometimes-but you do not find the difficulty outside-follows from the suggestion which many wildlife people have been making for a generation, namely, that there should be more migratory birds on the North American continent. This suggestion made by the wildlife people for as long as I can remember has always been turned down because of the fact that this wildlife was subsidized by farmers who had land around the various water holes which the ducks and geese use on their flights north and south. Here you have a clash. The wildlife people, advocating something that 20 million families in Canada desperately want, that is, more wildlife in the form of wild fowl or animals, are stymied by the fact that this increase in wildlife will be at the expense of the farmer whose income has not been growing in the same way that the income of other sections of the economy has been increasing.
As part of this general type of thinking, when I was in the United States I was made aware that the government there was planning an extensive move to take over much of the so-called wet lands in the United States to build up the wildlife population there. Their experts have made it clear to the government officials that the only way to do this properly was to spend most of the money in Canada. I made it clear on behalf of Canadian farmers that we would have to resist this move in Canada unless the bulk of this money went into the hands of the people who were providing the necessary ingredients for building up a wildlife population, namely the farmer. This argument was agreed to informally by the members of the United States government.
One of the items we discussed during the recent negotiations between the resource ministers of the two countries, the secretary for agriculture and myself was this question of how we could reconcile the needs of these two large segments of the population of our two countries and give an increase to the total wealth of this continent. Without going into all the details it was decided that we should set up a joint committee to examine the legal difficulties which lie in the way of having a joint operation between our two countries. It was decided that we should bring into this discussion the point of view of the farmers and the resource people to see if it would not be possible to take advantage of the large sums of money which are available from the supporters of wildlife, because it is those engaged in agriculture who are going to provide the food and shelter for these birds.
When I mention in this house that in North America approximately 70 per cent of the wild ducks are bred in the provinces of


Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta some hon. members may be surprised. These birds fly south along flyways to the gulf of Mexico and certain parts of the coasts of California and Florida. There is a real opportunity here to increase the income of farmers in the so-called pothole area of western Canada. In terms of square miles, 220,000 square miles of western Canada is so-called pothole country. If you take just the area of the potholes it is 2J million acres.
The great majority of farmers have looked on potholes as a nuisance and as a limiting factor in farming their land. If we can make these potholes an asset by having the sportsmen of this continent who want more ducks pay for these potholes and the grass around them and the grain planted to feed the ducks, what was once a liability to the farmers of western Canada could become an asset. These birds, as every biologist can confirm, are discriminatory feeders. If you plant a field of barley, wheat will not be touched by them. If you plant six-row barley, they will not eat that; they will just eat the two-row barley. Some birds like geese prefer corn to barley or wheat. Every biologist has known that for years.
No matter how silly some members of the opposition and some people across Canada think this idea is, the fact is that if you can add tens of millions of dollars a year to the income of farmers who have potholes-I do not care what these people think about this type of program-as long as you are increasing farm income you are achieving the results this bill was designed to achieve. I might mention, too, that I have discussed this matter with ministers of agriculture and resource ministers and they do not find it a silly idea. As a matter of fact, other provinces in addition to the prairie provinces have been taking an interest in this and wondering what can be done. There are three or four hundred thousand acres in the eastern provinces, I believe, which are amenable to this type of arrangement.
But that relates to just one of the hundreds of ideas in this bill to increase farm income and farm production. I shall not go into all the details of industrial development which is the part under rural development which intrigues most people.
It gave me great pleasure recently to go to Smith's Falls, in the county of Lanark, to preside at the opening of a new chocolate plant. That plant will cost some $7 million when completed, and will employ 200 or 300 people. It will utilize the milk of 1,000 good dairy cows. This is a perfect example of the increase in farm income opportunities in that

area, and the increase in the community income opportunities as a result of decentralization of an industry. This not only facilitates the income of the country but gives tangible help to the people in the rural areas. It is not an accident that, in many areas of the United Kingdom and the United States, where government legislation has provided this advantage to areas designated depressed, there has been an increase in the number of decentralized industries in these areas with resultant benefit, not only to the immediate areas, but to the whole country.
As my time is short, I should like now to give, to those who are serious students of conservation, some of the principles which will be followed in setting up this legislation. I am going to take the opportunity of outlining them in point form.
1.	While the program is focused mainly on farm people, it cannot be exclusively agricultural. Rural economies are no longer separate from town or urban economies, and the program must be one of area development embracing local centres of population as well as the farms surrounding them.
2.	The program should be regarded and accepted as long run rather than short run since many of the problems to be encountered are structural rather than either cyclical or transitory.
3.	The program should have two levels-a regional or local level; that is a local level within that region under the all-embracing framework of the national joint provincial-federal committee. Planning and action must be primarily local; the kind of action taken will depend on local resources and conditions.
While success depends upon local leadership, a national program directorate is essential for research, assistance in selecting personnel, and financing co-ordination of plans of various local programs, and to record and make available the experience of local programs to other local areas. The leadership must be primarily under the control of the provincial-federal directorate.
4.	The co-operation of provincial governments, universities, farm organizations, and other bodies, is essential, but it is important that the national program directorate take the lead in co-ordinating any activities of these bodies. It would be undesirable to have several unco-ordinated programs proceeding simultaneously and in isolation, under provincial, university or other leadership. The national directorate should maintain the position of leadership in all activities which are not local.
5.	The program may at times be closely related to other federal programs such as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act and the farm
Marginal Lands Development credit corporation, as well as, of course, to provincial extension and educational programs.
6.	It must be recognized at the outset that the problems of marginal areas and of programs developed to relieve these problems will be social as much as economic, political or technological. This in itself makes it essential to regard the program as a long run one, and to recognize the difficulties which it will encounter.
Those six principles outline the relative stages of control and direction which must be included in an attempt to extend this act successfully.
(1)	The action on this program will consist initially of the identification of marginal regions and of local development areas. This involves several important steps, (a) First, the selection of criteria by which we identify these regional redevelopment areas. I might add, in passing, that the best criterion we have is the income level of the areas.
(b) The second criterion is the regional redevelopment areas which will normally not coincide with local development areas, as the regions can be identified only on the basis of municipal statistics, whereas the local development areas will probably be smaller and based primarily upon local trade areas such as watersheds and perhaps municipal units, (c) The third criterion is that local areas have an optimum size-if too small, the resource base is likely to be inadequate; if too large, the problems of local leadership and organization would be excessive. That means in plain English that in some cases you will have several communities in the regional area, but within these several communities you will probably have several local development areas.
(2)	The second action on the program will be the selection of a limited number of local development areas, attempting to choose those which could provide an example to later programs in somewhat similar areas.
(3)	The third step in the action program would be the appointing of a field man from the national directorate who must attempt to stimulate interest by leaders in the local development area and to act only as their adviser, not leader. The transfer of initiative and leadership from a non-local to a local basis is difficult but very important, and must be achieved at a very early stage. Of course, a local development committee probably would consist of representatives of various farm organizations and boards of trade, churches, and so on.
(4)	The fourth step would involve the duties of the local development committee. The duties I have listed are: (a) to delineate the local development area; (b) to discuss

Mr. Chairman, now that we have the bill I think certain observations of a general character should be made, particularly in the light of the speech by the minister to which we have just listened. The bill bears examination, especially in the light of the claims made by the minister.
One would think from what the minister has said tonight and what he has been saying throughout the country since this measure first came forward that the government was embarking on a program that would in effect have immediate application. The first clause in the preamble to the bill reads as follows:
Whereas agriculture in Canada is undergoing technological changes that necessitate adjustments on the part of many Canadians engaged in this basic industry in order to maintain or raise their standard of living;
The bill at this moment does not do anything whatsoever to raise the standard of living of the farmers of Canada. Yet the minister has not indicated the long term character of the bill. He has given the impression wherever he has gone, including Smith's Falls, the last place on his tour throughout the nation, that the government has brought forward an agricultural program of which this is an important phase, something that is going to meet the problems of the farmers. I have carefully read the reports of the speeches of the minister as contained in the local and national press and nowhere will there be found any reference to the long term character of the bill.
What the government is doing, through the minister, in this matter, and let there be no mistake about it, is to bring forward another legislative enactment that will enable the propagandists of the government, of whom the minister is perhaps the most efficient next to the Prime Minister, to say, "Here is what we have done. We have brought forward a productivity bill. We brought forward a bill to provide for vocational grants to disabled people. We brought forward a bill to assist small business." And so on and so on.

speechtext:
The minister says this plan arose out of a statement made by the Prime Minister in announcing his charter for the farmers of Canada in 1957. The minister, no matter what contrivance he resorts to, stands convicted by the very pamphlet which he says represents not only the offer of this government but pays proper tribute to the work of the previous administration and the national farm organizations. The Minister of Agriculture has spent quite a bit of his time outside the house in the last few weeks enunciating this program. I think that from now on he should be on his guard because everything he has said is being carefully read by the members of this house. From now on, we will ascertain whether or not the Minister of Agriculture is really interested in the rehabilitation of agriculture or in the rehabilitation of his party which is continually losing public esteem and support in this country.
When the minister presented the resolution which preceded this bill, he said that what he wanted to do was to see the bill placed in the hands of provincial governments and certain national farm organizations for the purpose of eliciting their views. This was a commendable decision of the minister. We certainly have not had from the minister tonight any report of the nature of his conferences with the provincial ministers of agriculture or the governments of the provinces. We have had from the minister tonight only a vague reference to conferences with the provinces and with certain ministers of agriculture. We have not been told which ministers of agriculture. We have not been told if all the provinces and their departments of agriculture have been consulted. We have been told there was a conference in which the provinces indicated their willingness to co-operate.
What provincial governments, presented with legislation in these general terms, would take any other position than to say they would co-operate with this government in the prosecution and in the realization of the kind of measures envisaged in this particular enactment? What province would deny that it was prepared to give consideration to entering into an agreement with the federal government for the purpose of undertaking projects for more efficient use and economic development of marginal or submarginal agricultural lands? There is no obligation imposed on the province by that kind of language. Of course, the provinces are in favour of that. Just as everyone is against sin, so are the provinces in favour of trying to do something for agriculture.

But the minister has not given us any indication of the kind of specific agreement into which any particular province is prepared to enter. This bill came before this house in this form on March 23. When was the bill given to the provinces? When did this conference with the ministers of agriculture take place? Was it a general conference? Were there conferences with the two national farm organizations, and when did these conferences take place? The minister has not given us any indication whatever of the extent to which the provinces were willing to co-operate. He has not given us any indication as to how much money any particular province was prepared to commit itself to, in connection with this measure or in connection with any particular phase of this measure. All he has told us in this most general way is that, as a result of these conferences, so carelessly and so vaguely referred to, he has received an assurance from the provinces that there would be co-operation. We were told years ago this kind of co-operation would be given by the provinces with regard to the government's crop insurance legislation. All we have now as a result of that legislation is that one province has fully committed itself to an agreement and another has partially committed itself.
The minister cannot hope this parliament will take seriously his statement that the provinces have entered into any kind of commitment with regard to any particular phase of this bill. All that they have done, on the basis of the minister's own words, is to promise to co-operate, whatever that means. The minister does not indicate that the value of this bill is to be determined not in the light of what may happen today but what may happen some time in the unforeseeable future. The minister has not given us any indication when the first agreement under any one of these clauses, 3, 4 or 5, will begin. Will there be an agreement of any kind this year with respect to any of the provisions of these various clauses? Will there be an agreement next year? When will there be an agreement? Will there be an agreement in the next quarter century?
The minister has not given the committee any kind of assurance whatever. There is no obligation imposed on the government. If one examines clause 3 one finds there that the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council enter into a certain kind of agreement with any province providing for a joint arrangement. Then in clause 4 again the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, enter into an agreement

with any province providing for an undertaking jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof for the purpose of certain things such as agreements for soil improvement and water conservation projects.
Then there is provision that the minister may cause to be prepared and undertaken directly or in co-operation with the government of any province or any agency thereof programs of research and investigation, as if that is something that is unique and something new. That is being done now. Surely the minister knows that in his department there is a research division. The minister surely knows now that in that research division, research on land use and on other phases of agricultural interest are now being pursued. This legislation is not required to cause that to be done. Therefore this particular clause is nothing more than window dressing that flows from the mouth of the minister all intended for one purpose, namely to fail to disclose to the farmers of this country that this government, having promised so much to the farmers of Canada, has not been able to implement those promises.

I therefore do not think that anyone can say that this bill does what the minister in the generality of his language suggested it does. If the minister wishes to convince this house, the farmers and the people of Canada that this is a program designed for their immediate or shortterm amelioration let the minister say so. Let him give evidence of it. Let him produce evidence that there is at least some commitment by the provinces for sharing with the federal government in the cost of the projects that are envisaged. We have not even had from the minister any indication, except again in very general terms, of the nature of the cost-sharing plans. He told us that some of these plans would be on a 50-50 basis and that some would be on the basis of the extension of credit by either one of two senior governments or by both. But that again is so general as not to convey any real meaning whatsoever. Let the minister tell us that there is one province in connection with which there is a definite commitment for the federal government to expend X percentage of dollars and for the province to expend X percentage of dollars. Let him give us one example of that kind. Then he will be justified in the glowing references he makes to this new phase of the government's agricultural program.
This bill is like so many other projects of this government, Mr. Chairman. It reminds one of the Clark report that is still being studied by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. That is something for the long term. It reminds one of the legislation to which I made reference a moment ago, namely the legislation providing for grants for vocational rehabilitation. The bill introduced this session by the responsible minister in connection with that matter, as he was forced to admit, did not do anything whatsoever except to put in the form of an act something which was now being done and which had been done by governments for over a decade as the result of government policy formulated 12 years ago.

I say that the principle behind this bill is sound. I say that the principle behind this bill is good. There must be provision for agricultural rehabilitation, for further policies in the matter of land use, for policies designed to deal with the serious and critical situation that attends the farmers of Canada on marginal land. No one in this chamber quarrels with that objective. That was why the former government caused the committee in the other place to go into this whole matter, namely so that we could have the basis for some legislation in that regard. To the Minister of Agriculture I say this. By the pamphlet which he has distributed; by the speeches which he made to farm groups, particularly the speech he made the other day in Esquimalt-Saanich and the speech he made the other day in Smith's Falls, he has not added to his prestige nor to the prestige of his government.

The Liberal party has never brought into this house legislation which on its face was so far removed from the declarations of intention of the proposers or of the government. I doubt that you will find on our statutes any bill of this character, a bill that provides the government with powers which it may or may not exercise some time in the long future. I doubt that there is to be found on the statute book of our country any bill of this character. When the former government had a policy to bring forward, it brought in a specific enactment providing for something to be done forthwith, not something to be done in the long future. In this bill there is no guarantee that anything whatsoever will be done this year, next year or at any time. No obligation is imposed on this government to do anything. The only real purpose of the government in bringing forward this bill at this time in this form is to

add to the facade of political deception that it is creating throughout this country by trying to give the impression that it has accomplished something when in fact it has failed in the discharge of its promises made to the Canadian people in two general elections. That is the real situation. The minister could rise now and tell me, tell the committee, if the hon. member for Essex East is wrong. He could say, "Here is what we have done; we have an agreement with the province of X to do thus and thus at a certain time." I challenge the minister now to give us one bit of evidence that he has a specific agreement with any province pursuant to any clause of this bill.

Well, I don't know. If he keeps on, maybe he will be doing just that. His job is to improve the fortunes of the Conservative party in rural Canada and he has decided that in order to do that he must be out and about the country for a very large part of the time. I understand that the minister in closing the debate-I was not here at that time, though I heard about his closing remarks-made a long reference to some of the things I have said on this subject and on other subjects. I am highly pleased he should have taken the trouble to deal with some of the statements I have made. I hope he will order a large number of copies of Hansard for today and send them out across western Canada. I particularly invite him to send them to my own constituency since he has spent so much time dealing with remarks which have been made from this corner of the house.
The hon. member for Essex East endeavoured to demonstrate that while there is nothing in this legislation, members of the Liberal party really had had a policy of their own with respect to conservation. Their policy, as the hon. member so well pointed out, was to appoint a committee of the other place some four years ago to undertake what seems to be a permanent study of land use in this country. The present approach may not be the best approach in the world but I think it is far better to have an act, even an inadequate act, placed before the House of Commons than to have a long, almost endless study going on in the other place. I think the hon. member for Essex East might have improved his argument a great deal if he had pointed out some of the things which the minister of agriculture in the former administration had done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act rather than referring only to the program of study which was undertaken in the other place.
I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture whether any agreements whatsoever are pending with the provinces. I should like to hear from the minister whether he expects any agreement at all to be signed this year and, if so, how many agreements and in what form he expects them to be signed. This whole bill, with the exception of the research features, is dependent upon provincial agreement and co-operation. I see nothing in this bill-and let the minister correct me if I am wrong-which permits the federal government to undertake projects with the farmers to bring about certain desired improvements in income or certain desired changes in land use.
As I say, every clause of this bill is dependent upon provincial agreement. In other words, the federal government is taking no
Marginal Lands Development direct responsibility on its own. Its responsibility will be exercised only by agreement with the provinces. I think there is a place for agreement with the provinces. There is probably a place for agreement with the provinces in every clause of the bill. But I submit there is also room for direct agreements with the farmers concerned in order that the federal government in co-operation with farmers may do something to increase farm income. I see no such provision here. I do not know why the bill has been prepared in this way. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act provided that the federal government could undertake direct projects. Section 9 of that act reads as follows:
The minister may, subject to section 4-
That has to do with recommendations of advisory committees.
-undertake the development, construction, promotion, operation and maintenance of any project or scheme under or by virtue of this act or enter into any agreement with any province, municipality or person with respect thereto.
In other words, under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act the federal government is given power to deal directly with farmers and this the federal government has done in thousands of instances. It has provided direct assistance to farmers in connection with dug-outs, stock watering dams and other projects. However, under this so-called A.R.D.A. program no direct benefit goes to the farmers, as I read it. First of all, there has to be a master agreement with the provinces relating to those projects. I suggest that if it is claiming all the initiative it is now, in this field the federal government should show the same kind of initiative as is set forth in section 9 of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act so that the federal government in consultation and agreement with the provinces might go out and do a job of raising farm income.
No one can be fully sure of what can be accomplished under this measure. Certainly within the provisions of the measure there is room and possibility for broad beneficial results. No one can tell from reading this measure whether it is going to be a part of the vision, part of a political propaganda splurge, or whether it will mean something very positive and worth while in the way of government policy.
Farmers have been disappointed in the past. This government introduced a measure in 1948, referred to as Bill No. 237, which proposed legislation under which farmers were assured that the government guaranteed floor prices for nine main agricultural commodities. They have found out since that these floor prices are very largely fictitious, and that it is very difficult, by means of the deficiency payment formula, to obtain any

The minister has referred to projects which will be financed on a 50-50 basis. I should like to ask the minister whether he can name one project in regard to which he expects to sign an agreement with any province, financed on a 50-50 basis? He has also referred to a 37J-37J-25 division. I should like to ask the minister whether he can inform this committee of any project that will be financed in that way?
The minister has also referred to certain projects regarding the seeding of land to barley, as I understood him, for wildlife, such as ducks. I should be very interested to learn from the minister how this project will work out in practice. I know that tens of thousands of farmers in western Canada have lost many fields of grain, particularly barley, year after year, because of ducks. The ducks land in vast numbers in a field of barley and destroy that field of barley in a matter of hours. I should like to know whether there is any provision in this bill, as it is now drafted, to compensate farmers for the destruction of their fields of barley by ducks, or is this a special provision in respect of special land seeded to barley to provide feed for wildlife?
Mr. Chairman, as I have said, the value of this measure can be determined only by the action taken by both federal and provincial governments, and I should think the members of this committee would be interested in learning whether, under this legislation, the government expects to have any project in operation during the present calendar year and, if so, which project will it be.

However, the hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that the federal government could not, by itself directly, do anything for the farmers. I suggest that is the normal type of comment which results from the thinking of that group of which he is a member. He had reference, as I understood it, to the decentralization of control. I think it is quite clear that the terms of the bill indicate recognition of the fact that the best way to work out the problem is by co-operating with local authorities who know best those lines of approach which are most suited to their particular areas. I do not think the mighty know-it-alls of Ottawa are in a position to do that. I realize the C.C.F. party, in the past, has felt that all good things and all knowledge flow from Ottawa. I have found, through consultation with members of the party to which I belong, that it is generally our opinion that matters such as those involved here are best decided and appraised by the local people who are directly concerned and possess greater local knowledge. Of course, it is the policy of the federal government to assist and participate in these matters.
I should like to make a suggestion to the minister in respect of A.R.D.A. I do so in answer to the suggestions made by the previous speakers that the minister has not mentioned specific projects to any extent having relation to the establishment of farmers' markets. Farmers' markets have been considered as poor relations. To a large degree they have been ignored by large farm organizations and perhaps by branches of government because they do not fit into the modern concept of big business and the like.
The farmers' market is a ready-made established form of small farm help. It needs only more backing, understanding and promotion from agricultural and provincial and municipal authorities. A number of hon. members may be uninformed on farm markets because in large urban areas they are not in evidence at the present time. They are much in evidence in smaller semi-urban and rural areas. My submission, Mr. Chairman, is that they could be promoted in the larger areas to the benefit of small farmers.
Each vendor in the farmers' market represents a small independent business. In other words, each farmers' market is a collection of small independent farmer businessmen. For the benefit of members who perhaps have not those farm markets in their area I would mention that it is normally the custom to hold one of those markets once a week, ordinarily on Saturdays, or sometimes two or three times a week, depending on the area concerned.
Marginal Lands Development
The primary users of farmers' markets are first of all market gardeners and also fruit growers with limited capital and acreage who for reasons of age are perhaps not able to expand in today's stepped up economy or perhaps, as I have said, they do not have the capital to do so. Another group who use farmers' markets are small farmers selling everything from maple syrup to cabbage to supplement their incomes. A third group are the wives of mixed family farmers who sell poultry products and home baking for the obvious purpose again of supplementing the family income. The two other groups that customarily use farmers' markets are farmer butchers and hucksters. I know a number of people say that hucksters have no place in farmers' markets. They buy produce of the farms and go and sell it themselves on the market. But after all, hucksters have to make a living, too.
The first three groups are, I think, perhaps the most important, namely the market gardeners and the small farmers who are selling produce to supplement their income and the wives of mixed farmers who sell poultry and home baking.
What function does the farmers' market perform in a community? Well, first of all it provides fresh produce directly from the producer to the consumer, and in these days this is something very beneficial because many vegetables which the large grocery chains and other organizations sell to the public are picked, sent to a large centre and sorted and redistributed. By the time the public gets them they are not always in the best of condition. This, of course, is particularly applicable to vegetables such as asparagus and sweet corn. Thus, the first function that the market can perform is to see that the people in the area are provided with fresh produce direct from the producer to the consumer.
The second thing is that the community itself derives value from the market. Of course, there is a little extra business from the farmers who come in on Saturday or Wednesday market days. A very important thing it does is to promote good urban-rural relations. This, Mr. Chairman, is a most important function of the farmers' market.
In the city in whieh I live, namely Woodstock, there has been a large and active farm market ever since I can remember. It is an event that most people in the city look forward to every Saturday. They look forward with keen interest to coming down to the market and exchanging ideas and having a talk with their friends from the country who bring in the various kinds of produce. I know everyone looks forward to it. This, of course,

Marginal Lands Development leads to a mutual understanding of rural-urban problems. This is something which cannot be measured in dollars and cents. It has great intangible values. It is a one-day attraction, but it is also a tourist attraction. I know of people who occasionally visit our town from large areas who get quite a kick out of going down to the market and seeing first hand the farm produce brought in. Tourists from other countries also go down town to see the market. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be a very good idea if everything were done to retain and if possible expand this multitude of small enterprises in farmers' markets.
I should like just briefly to give the committee some figures to show how farm income can be supplemented by the use of the farm market. Might I say that these figures were given to me by Mrs. Alec Cureton who lives in the county in my area and who keeps a very exact cost accounting of her week's operations. The first item of expense that she mentions is something that I want to refer to again in a moment. The rent for the stall comes to $2.50 each Saturday. The cost of bags comes to 34 cents and boxes, 60 cents. The cost of bringing the truck in amounts to $1. Therefore, her total cost is $4.44. These are her actual revenue figures for one week: 49 dozen eggs, $23.85. I might say that this revenue was for the week ended May 6. The cost of producing the eggs-in other words, the feed-came to $17.20; the balance before other costs would be $6.65. For four bags of potatoes she received $11.30. The cost of producing those potatoes was $8 and the profit, $3.30. For 63 boxes of flowers, pansies, she received $20.60. For three bird houses made from scrap lumber she received $2.25. The gross income was $32.80. The net cost was $4.44, leaving a balance of $28.36. This is not a great deal of money when one considers the work involved, but I have talked frequently to this particular vendor and many others in the local market and they are very glad indeed to be able to have this supplementary income which greatly assists them in being able to carry on.
How can farm markets be improved and expanded? First of all, there should be strong support and backing from the Department of Agriculture by means of promotion and the like. Second, the Minister of Agriculture mentioned earlier this evening education of local authorities by means of literature and the press on the value of farm markets for A.R.D.A. Third, and of most importance perhaps in practical terms, co-operation with provincial and municipal authorities in improving and expanding farm markets as a part of A.R.D.A. and-here is the important thing-as a public service.


Originally, farmers' markets were intended as a service to the district farmers and indeed to the citizens of the towns and cities. They were not intended as a money-making scheme as some people and indeed some municipal councils think. I mention this because I know that in some areas there has been a tendency for municipal councils to raise the rents for farmers coming in on Saturdays or on Wednesdays as the case may be. I would point out that the intention of those markets was not to be money making but to provide a service. Since we all know that in the last 15 years costs have risen gradually, to raise the rents for farmers who come in on Saturdays when the price of their produce has not increased greatly would work a great hardship. It is in this way that the federal government could contribute to the expansion and promotion of farm markets through provincial and municipal authorities.
This is a project that I think could be greatly expanded to everybody's benefit. It provides the small family farmer and his wife with additional income which is very badly needed to purchase those little extra things they might not otherwise be able to get. At the same time, as I have already mentioned, it promotes good urban-rural relations and provides the public with good, fresh produce which they perhaps cannot otherwise get in some of the large cities.
I know that a number of places such as Hamilton, London, Kitchener and others have very fine markets indeed. They provide a great service to these communities. These are medium to large size cities, and I know that in smaller cities such as Woodstock from which I come such markets are also very popular. I think this idea could be expanded into the larger urban municipalities to the great advantage of both the rural and urban population.

I should like to emphasize one point, namely, that each of us agreed that it is wise to do our research ahead of time rather than to go ahead and blunder into mistakes. Therefore I think the first thing you will see is a series of research agreements outlining certain areas and problems.
With regard to the second question having to do with making arrangements directly with the farmers, the legislation specifies that agreements may be made with a province or any agency thereof. As the federal government we have the feeling that when we are dealing with matters affecting property and civil rights the provinces should either be partners with us or should name some group with which we can be partners. Under the legislation the province will have to designate the agency. I would suggest that in certain provinces it might be a conservation district while in others it might be a municipality. If a group of people organize themselves into a particular district for a specific purpose, there is nothing to stop the province from authorizing them as the agency, and that is the reason for drafting the legislation in this way.

I am glad the hon. member has brought the issue out so clearly because it gives me a chance to explain very simply, and in blunt terms, what the hon. member should have learned here in the last 15 years. If he goes back and reads the words of the man of whom he spoke so highly here a week ago Saturday, Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner and his great contributions to P.F.R.A., he will find that Mr. Gardiner made a very clear statement on this particular subject on May 22, 1947, just exactly 14 years ago today.
Now, the minister of agriculture at that time had been asked to extend the principles of P.F.R.A. into other provinces. This is his statement, as reported on page 3317 of Hansard of that day:
I am now authorized to make the following statement of present policy.
The present Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act will be continued as applicable to the established P.F.R.A. area in the three prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
This act was passed in 1935 and amended in 1937, 1939 and 1941. It provides that works may be undertaken to rehabilitate certain areas in the prairie provinces even though the constitutional position is that such works are the responsibility of the province or municipality. There were, however. a number of special circumstances which justified P.F.R.A. Included in these is the fact that the dominion government administered the lands and resources of the area during its period of settlement and the further fact that there was reason to believe at that time that a very large area was subject to drought so severe and of such long duration as to make permanent residence difficult if not impossible without conservation and distribution of water.
He then goes on to describe the details, with which I shall not deal. However, he continues further along:
It has been suggested that because of the benefits already apparent in the area to which P.F.R.A. has been applied, the principles of the act should be extended by legislation to all other parts of Canada.
In view of the constitutional relationship between the dominion and the provinces the government has decided that such legislation should not be recommended. It is held that the same obligation does not exist in other parts of the prairie provinces or in the remainder of Canada as in the drought area of the prairie provinces.

It is considered, however, that there are certain works outside the drought area which if undertaken would be of assistance to all Canada through making possible increased development of farm lands which if left to provincial or municipal responsibility might greatly retard Canada's development.
Then, he goes on to describe what those increased activities could be, with a special program of marshland development in the maritimes and farm lands in British Columbia, and so on. The essential point which he makes, which is constitutionally sound, is that this matter of conservation is in the hands of the provincial governments. It was only due to the special circumstance that the land of the prairie provinces was so long under the federal government which had followed policies which allowed the land to be denuded that made it necessary for the Conservative government in 1935 to introduce this very fine legislation, and thus get around the constitutional position. These resources had only been turned back to the provincial governments in 1931.
I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that under this measure we can give assistance to farmers if a province designates that group of farmers as an agency of that province.

The minister says the constitution is applied in this way in the prairies because of drought conditions and because the land was in the hands of the federal government for such a long period of time. Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and for the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Tomorrow we will start with No. 5 on today's order paper which is Bill No. C-92, to amend the Criminal Code. If that business is completed we will continue with Bill No. C-77, having to do with agricultural development. Then there are three other legislative items which are available if time permits. They are No. 6 on today's order paper, Bill No. C-97 to amend the Combines Investigation Act, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Justice concerning the Judges Act and the Exchequer Court Act and the resolution in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to the Export Credits Insurance Act.
For Wednesday, I am assuming we complete the debate on the amendments to the Criminal Code; if we are close to finishing that on Tuesday night but have not completed it we might consider it advisable to do that on Wednesday. After that is finished we would begin with the estimates of the Department of Justice on Wednesday and then, by consultation and arrangement, the house might go on with the estimates of the Department of Health and Welfare on Thursday and revert on Friday and Saturday to the estimates of the Secretary of State and of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.
It being three minutes after 10.30 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.

Tuesday, May 23, 1961
